CONTENT PRACTICE

One release. More than one story.

A practical way to turn a product change into a post, an article, and useful release notes.

Clara · Abstract Machines

ONE IDEA / THREE WAYS
The post. ↗The story. ≡The details. +

Start with one source of truth

Before choosing a format, write down what changed. Who can use it? What is different in their day? What are the limits? Keep those answers together with the supporting product material. Every piece in the launch should agree on these facts.

Imagine a fictional project tool adding a shared overview. The feature is a view of the work across a team. The useful story might be that people can see what needs their attention without collecting individual updates.

Give the social post one job

A social post can introduce the problem and the change. Choose one recognizable situation, explain the improvement, and give the reader somewhere to go next. It doesn’t need to carry the entire specification.

For our fictional tool, the opening could describe the time spent asking for status updates. The rest of the post can explain how the overview brings those updates together. Keep the promise within what the product actually does.

Let the article do the explaining

An article has room for a worked example. Show the old workflow, walk through the new one, and explain when someone would use it. Screenshots or a short visual sequence can make that change easier to follow.

Include the details that help a reader decide whether to try it. If setup is required or only certain projects are supported, say so where it matters.

Keep release notes precise

Existing users need a direct account of what changed and how to find it. Use the actual feature name, describe its availability, and link to the relevant instructions. This is where precision earns more trust than a memorable headline.

Review the pieces together

Read the post, article, and release notes side by side. Do the names match? Are the claims consistent? Does each piece serve its audience? A connected launch should feel like one product story expressed at different levels of detail.

In Clara, campaign plays help keep related work together. Begin with the same product context, brief each piece for its purpose, then review the set before sharing.
